world_letter_writing_day.label: World Letter Writing Day
world_letter_writing_day.intro: A nudge to pick up a pen instead of a phone. A handwritten letter takes longer, costs a stamp and gets kept in a drawer for years, which is exactly the point.
funFacts: The day goes back to Australian artist Richard Simpkin, who spent years handwriting letters to people he admired.
Some of the oldest surviving letters are clay tablets from Mesopotamian traders, written roughly 4,000 years ago.
The Penny Black of 1840 was the first adhesive postage stamp and made sending a letter affordable for almost everyone.

world_coconut_day.label: World Coconut Day
world_coconut_day.intro: A day for the palm that supplies food, drink, oil, rope and roofing all at once. In coconut-growing countries it is celebrated with markets, fairs and a lot of fresh coconut water.
funFacts: It has been marked on 2 September since 2009, the founding date of the community of coconut-producing countries.
Botanically a coconut is not a nut but a drupe, which makes it a relative of plums and cherries.
Coconuts float and stay able to sprout after weeks at sea, which is how palms colonised tropical coastlines.

skyscraper_day.label: Skyscraper Day
skyscraper_day.intro: A day to crane your neck. Skyscrapers turned cities upward, and every generation has tried to build one taller than the last.
funFacts: The date is the birthday of architect Louis Sullivan, born on 3 September 1856 and known for the maxim 'form follows function'.
Chicago's ten-storey Home Insurance Building of 1885 is widely called the first skyscraper thanks to its steel frame.
The Burj Khalifa in Dubai has held the height record since 2010 at 828 metres.

macadamia_nut_day.label: National Macadamia Nut Day
macadamia_nut_day.intro: A tribute to the buttery nut that grows on Australian rainforest trees. Rich, mild and famously hard to crack, which is why it usually arrives ready shelled.
funFacts: Macadamias are native to Australian rainforests and were named after the chemist John Macadam.
Their shells are among the toughest of any nut, so most macadamias are sold already cracked.
Hawaii became the centre of commercial growing after macadamia trees were planted there in the 1880s.

be_late_for_something_day.label: Be Late for Something Day
be_late_for_something_day.intro: Official permission to stop rushing for once. The idea is not chronic tardiness but a few unhurried minutes: look around, finish the coffee, arrive slightly late and unbothered.
funFacts: The day was created by the Procrastinators' Club of America, founded in Philadelphia in 1956 by Les Waas.
Club founder Les Waas also wrote the jingle for the Mister Softee ice cream vans heard across the United States.
German universities still use the 'academic quarter': a lecture at nine actually starts at a quarter past.

read_a_book_day.label: Read a Book Day
read_a_book_day.intro: A day with a very simple instruction: open a book and read it. No app, no notifications, just one story and however many pages you manage.
funFacts: Johannes Gutenberg's printing press of around 1450 turned books from rare treasures into everyday objects.
The Library of Congress is the world's largest library, holding well over 170 million items.
Iceland has the jolabokaflod, a Christmas book flood: books are given on 24 December and read the same night.

salami_day.label: National Salami Day
salami_day.intro: A day for the sausage that keeps. Air-dried, spiced and sliced thin, salami was preserving meat centuries before anyone owned a fridge.
funFacts: The name comes from the Italian verb salare, to salt, the technique that made the sausage keep without cooling.
Salami ripens by fermenting and drying, and the pale coating on the skin is an edible noble mould.
Italy alone protects dozens of regional salami by law, from Milano to Felino and the small cacciatore sausages.

star_trek_day.label: Star Trek Day
star_trek_day.intro: The anniversary of the day the Enterprise first appeared on television. Fans celebrate with marathons, conventions and an unreasonable number of pointed ears.
funFacts: The first episode, 'The Man Trap', was broadcast on 8 September 1966.
After a fan write-in campaign, NASA named its first space shuttle Enterprise in 1976.
Mobile phone pioneer Martin Cooper named the series' flip communicator as an inspiration for his handset design.

teddy_bear_day.label: Teddy Bear Day
teddy_bear_day.intro: A day for the one toy almost everybody had. Teddy bears get hugged flat, lose an eye and still end up in a box in the attic rather than the bin.
funFacts: The name goes back to US President Theodore 'Teddy' Roosevelt, who refused to shoot a tethered bear on a hunt in 1902.
Shopkeeper Morris Michtom put a stuffed bear in his New York window and asked Roosevelt for permission to call it a Teddy.
In Germany the Steiff company was making jointed toy bears at the same time, marked with the button in the ear from 1904.

tv_dinner_day.label: National TV Dinner Day
tv_dinner_day.intro: A nostalgic salute to dinner on a tray in front of the screen. The compartmented aluminium meal was 1950s convenience food and became a design icon by accident.
funFacts: Swanson launched the frozen tray meal in 1954 in a box printed to look like a television set.
Company lore says a huge surplus of unsold Thanksgiving turkey gave someone the idea in the first place.
An original Swanson tray is part of the collection of the Smithsonian in Washington.

hot_cross_bun_day.label: National Hot Cross Bun Day
hot_cross_bun_day.intro: A day for the spiced sweet bun with a cross on top. Traditionally British and traditionally Easter, but nobody has ever objected to eating one in September.
funFacts: Hot cross buns are enriched with spices and dried fruit, and the cross is usually piped on in flour paste.
A London decree of 1592 limited their sale to burials, Good Friday and Christmas, which made them a treat.
Folklore claimed a bun baked on Good Friday would never go mouldy, so sailors took them to sea for luck.

video_games_day.label: National Video Games Day
video_games_day.intro: A day to stop apologising for playing. Console, arcade cabinet or phone, the point is the same: a small world with rules you can actually win.
funFacts: Physicist William Higinbotham built Tennis for Two on an oscilloscope in 1958 to entertain visitors to his laboratory.
Pong made arcade machines mainstream in 1972, and early cabinets reportedly broke down because the coin boxes overflowed.
Tetris was written by Alexey Pajitnov in Moscow in 1984 and reached the West only after a tangle of licence deals.

roald_dahl_day.label: Roald Dahl Day
roald_dahl_day.intro: The birthday of the author behind Matilda, the BFG and the chocolate factory. Schools and libraries mark it with readings, costumes and a lot of invented vocabulary.
funFacts: Roald Dahl was born on 13 September 1916 in Llandaff in Wales to Norwegian parents.
He wrote in a small hut in his garden, on yellow paper, with six pencils sharpened before every session.
After his son's accident he helped develop the Wade-Dahl-Till valve, used to treat fluid on the brain.

cream_filled_donut_day.label: National Cream-Filled Donut Day
cream_filled_donut_day.intro: A day for the doughnut with no hole, because something better is hiding inside. Custard, whipped cream or jam, eaten in one go over a plate.
funFacts: By legend the hole in the ring doughnut was invented by American sailor Hanson Gregory in the 19th century.
The Boston cream doughnut has been the official state doughnut of Massachusetts since 2003.
Germany's Berliner and Austria's Krapfen are the same idea without the ring: filled, fried and dusted with sugar.

linguine_day.label: National Linguine Day
linguine_day.intro: A day for the flat cousin of spaghetti. Slightly wider, slightly chewier and unbeatable with clams, seafood or a spoonful of green pesto.
funFacts: Linguine means 'little tongues' in Italian, a nod to the flattened cross section of the strands.
The shape comes from Liguria, the same coastal region that gave the world basil pesto.
Italy uses hundreds of pasta shapes, each matched to how well it carries a particular sauce.

guacamole_day.label: National Guacamole Day
guacamole_day.intro: A day for the green dip that turns a bowl of tortilla chips into a meal. Avocado, lime, salt, and endless arguments about whether onion belongs in it.
funFacts: The word comes from the Nahuatl ahuacamolli, avocado sauce, and the dish was already eaten in Aztec Mexico.
Avocados only ripen after they are picked, so growers can use the tree itself as a natural storeroom.
Every Hass avocado descends from a single seedling grown by postman Rudolph Hass in California in the 1920s.

apple_dumpling_day.label: National Apple Dumpling Day
apple_dumpling_day.intro: A whole apple, cored, filled with sugar and cinnamon and baked in a pastry coat. Autumn comfort food that fills the kitchen with the smell of the season.
funFacts: Apple dumplings are a Pennsylvania Dutch farmhouse classic and were once served for breakfast as often as dessert.
More than 7,500 apple cultivars are grown worldwide, but only a couple of dozen make it into supermarkets.
Apples float because roughly a quarter of their volume is air, which is what makes apple bobbing possible.

world_bamboo_day.label: World Bamboo Day
world_bamboo_day.intro: A day for the plant that builds houses, scaffolding, floors, bicycles and dinner. Bamboo grows back faster than almost anything else you can build with.
funFacts: The day was declared in 2009 at the 8th World Bamboo Congress in Bangkok.
Bamboo is a grass, not a tree, and the fastest species can add up to 90 centimetres in a single day.
In Hong Kong, bamboo scaffolding is still tied together by hand around high-rise construction sites.

talk_like_a_pirate_day.label: International Talk Like a Pirate Day
talk_like_a_pirate_day.intro: One day a year when 'arrr' counts as a complete sentence. Offices, radio stations and schools join in, and nobody has to explain themselves.
funFacts: Two friends from Oregon, John Baur and Mark Summers, invented the day in 1995 while playing racquetball.
It went worldwide in 2002 after American columnist Dave Barry wrote about it in his newspaper column.
The classic pirate growl largely comes from actor Robert Newton's Long John Silver in the 1950 film Treasure Island.

punch_day.label: National Punch Day
punch_day.intro: A day for the big shared bowl. Punch was the original party drink, ladled out for a whole room long before anyone shook a cocktail for one.
funFacts: The name is usually traced to the Hindi word for five, for the five parts: spirit, sugar, lemon, water and spice.
Sailors and traders of the East India Company brought the drink from India to Europe in the 17th century.
Georgian punch bowls could hold several litres and were passed around the table with a single large ladle.

miniature_golf_day.label: Miniature Golf Day
miniature_golf_day.intro: A day for windmills, loops and that one hole nobody ever manages in a single putt. Mini golf is golf with the walking, etiquette and expense removed.
funFacts: The Ladies' Putting Club at St Andrews, opened in 1867, is the oldest miniature golf course still in play.
Swiss architect Paul Bongni standardised the concrete course in 1954 and trademarked the name Minigolf.
It is a competitive sport with world championships, and players carry dozens of balls tuned for different obstacles.

hobbit_day.label: Hobbit Day
hobbit_day.intro: The shared birthday of Bilbo and Frodo Baggins. Fans celebrate by walking barefoot, eating far too much and reading a few chapters of Tolkien out loud.
funFacts: In the Shire Reckoning both Bilbo and Frodo were born on 22 September, which is where the date comes from.
The American Tolkien Society has promoted the day since 1978 as the centrepiece of Tolkien Week.
Hobbits are described as eating up to seven meals a day, second breakfast and elevenses included.

checkers_day.label: National Checkers Day
checkers_day.intro: A day for the board game that hides real depth behind twelve simple discs. Easy enough for a child in a minute, hard enough to keep adults arguing over one move.
funFacts: The modern game took shape in southern France around 1100, when pieces from the older game alquerque moved onto a chessboard.
English draughts is played on 64 squares, while international draughts uses a 100-square board and twenty pieces a side.
In 2007 the Chinook program solved English draughts: with perfect play by both sides the game always ends in a draw.

world_gorilla_day.label: World Gorilla Day
world_gorilla_day.intro: A day for our huge, quiet, plant-eating relatives. Gorillas live in close family groups, and the imposing silverback is mostly a very patient babysitter.
funFacts: The day began in 2017, on the fiftieth anniversary of Dian Fossey's Karisoke Research Center in Rwanda.
Gorillas share roughly 98 percent of their DNA with humans, making them among our closest living relatives.
Every gorilla has a unique pattern of wrinkles above the nose, which researchers use like a fingerprint.

comic_book_day.label: National Comic Book Day
comic_book_day.intro: A day for panels, speech bubbles and the shops that smell of paper. Superheroes, graphic novels and manga all count, and so does rereading the same issue again.
funFacts: Superman's debut in Action Comics No. 1 in 1938 launched the superhero genre; surviving copies now sell for millions.
In France and Belgium comics are called the ninth art, and Brussels has dozens of painted comic walls.
Japanese manga are read from right to left, and the weekly anthologies run to several hundred pages each.

better_breakfast_day.label: National Better Breakfast Day
better_breakfast_day.intro: A day to take the first meal seriously for once. Not cereal standing at the counter, but a proper table, a warm drink and ten unhurried minutes.
funFacts: Breakfast literally means breaking the overnight fast, and the French dejeuner and Spanish desayuno say exactly the same thing.
Cornflakes came out of the Kellogg brothers' sanatorium kitchen in the 1890s, from a batch of wheat left standing too long.
Breakfast looks wildly different around the world: rice congee in China, ful medames in Egypt, fresh rolls in Germany.

world_tourism_day.label: World Tourism Day
world_tourism_day.intro: A day for the pleasure of going somewhere else. Packing a bag, getting lost in an unfamiliar street and coming home with stories is one of life's cheapest luxuries.
funFacts: The day has been held since 1980 and marks the adoption of the world tourism organisation's statutes in 1970.
France has been the world's most visited country for decades, ahead of Spain and the United States.
The word tourist appeared in English around 1800, when the Grand Tour was the finishing school of the wealthy.

good_neighbor_day.label: National Good Neighbor Day
good_neighbor_day.intro: A day for the people who take in your parcels and water your plants. Neighbourliness is small, unglamorous and the reason a street feels like somewhere to live.
funFacts: The idea came from Becky Mattson of Lakeside, Montana, in the early 1970s; President Carter proclaimed the day in 1978.
The English word neighbour comes from Old English roots meaning roughly 'the near dweller'.
Fred Rogers opened his children's programme with 'Won't You Be My Neighbor?' for more than thirty years.

biscotti_day.label: National Biscotti Day
biscotti_day.intro: A day for the hard almond biscuit that is meant to be dunked. Coffee, tea or sweet wine, biscotti soften just enough and never fall apart in the cup.
funFacts: Biscotti means twice baked: the dough is baked as a loaf, sliced, then baked again until dry.
That dryness made them travel food, and hard twice-baked biscuits fed Roman soldiers and later sailors for months.
In Tuscany the almond version is called cantuccio and is traditionally dipped in sweet Vin Santo.

mulled_cider_day.label: National Hot Mulled Cider Day
mulled_cider_day.intro: A day for the mug that warms your hands. Apple juice or cider heated with cinnamon, cloves and orange, and suddenly the end of September feels cosy rather than grey.
funFacts: In North America cider means cloudy unfiltered apple juice, while in Britain it is the alcoholic drink.
Mulling means gently heating a drink with spices, the same method behind mulled wine.
It takes roughly three dozen apples to press a single gallon of cider, which is about four litres.
